utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. After days of sitting in Courtroom III, you tend to forget how intimate this particular courtroom is. May we have the appearances, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Good morning, Your Honours. Gramsci Di Fazio, Joanna Korner, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suppose the sight of me here, Your Honours, must have alerted you, if nothing else, to I have a couple of matters to raise, shortly, before the witness comes. The witness on any showing is to finish today because, as I understand it, there's only an hour's cross-examination to be engaged in. Your Honours, can I mention the question of the application that we've made to call the witnesses in respect of the disallowed or rejected adjudicated facts because the Defence responded yesterday on the 30th of June and there's just a couple of matters arising from that response that I wanted to mention. Your Honours, firstly, they say, in paragraph 5 of the response, that contrary to the provisions of Rule of 66(A)(ii) and the order pronounced orally by the Trial Chamber on the 11th of June, 2010, the Prosecution still failed to provide full disclosure in relation to any of the proposed witnesses. Now, the first matter, Your Honours, is that you -- your order of the 11th of June was that we should -- which I had here a moment ago, yes. It's in the transcript at page 11675 at the bottom and going over to the next page: For these reasons, the Chamber now orders the Prosecution to file an addendum with the summaries of the anticipated evidence of the proposed 57 - we counted some of them twice, so it's 53 now - by Wednesday, the 16th of June, and orders the Prosecution to provide status reports on the disclosure of material. And, Your Honours, that we did. So we would respectfully suggest we're not in breach of any orders made by Your Honours. The second matter is that the statement that the Prosecution has still failed to provide full disclosure in relation to any of the proposed witnesses is also erroneous in that as we said in our motion for 18 -- Your Honours, I need to find that. Yes. Your Honours, this is the -- our filing of the 17th of June to comply with the order. Under paragraph 5, Rule 66(A)(ii), disclosure, for each of the 50 witnesses identified, Prosecution has disclosed the Defence all prior witness statements and/or testimony found in the Prosecution's internal database. According to the Prosecution disclosure record, it's disclosed 66(A)(ii) material for 18 of the proposed witnesses, prior to the commencement of trial, because they were originally on our list. Your Honours, the reason I'm raising it today is that the Defence, apart from, we say, erroneously suggesting we're in breach of any order made by Your Honours, complain again that we should be doing full searches on all our proposed witnesses now. Your Honours, as a matter of policy, we do do these full searches, but they involve not only the lawyers in going through a massive material but involve a number of other sections within the OTP doing what are called these full ISU searches. I think Your Honours have heard the term before. Your Honours, we do say that that is a total waste of resources, and indeed an unnecessary burden on the Defence to receive such material is -- as we may give -- may discover if the -- if Your Honours are not going to allow us to call either all or some of the proposed witnesses. And so, Your Honours, the reason I'm raising it now is we really need to know fairly urgently what is to happen; whether Your Honours think that the Defence suggestions have merit or not, whether we're going to be allowed to call the witnesses or not. We've got three weeks left before the break. And so if Your Honours are going to order us in accordance with the Defence wishes to do these full searches, well, then -- before you make any ruling, then we need to know, as usually I suppose, asap. Your Honours, we would suggest, as I say, that it's a total waste of resources and is no assistance to the Defence, but we would ask either, if that is to be the situation, that you make that ruling today or tomorrow -- or not tomorrow; we're not sitting. Or, alternatively, we could have a decision on the witnesses. So that's the first matter that I want to raise. Your Honours, the second matter is allied, but I don't know if you want to hear from the Defence before I go on to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. I'll ask for your indulgence for me to address one preliminary matter and that is that we acknowledge and we empathise with Ms. Korner this morning, and perhaps the proper word is we sympathise with her, given the fact that today's a very special day. This is the -- this day's the anniversary of the day in which -- on which Ms. Korner came into the world. And so we understand how big an event it must be and it to be seen and reflected in her submissions. We will not, however, pursue the point of asking which anniversary it is; after all, we are in open session. But from our side of the room, we all wish her a very happy birthday. Thank you for your indulgence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the Chamber joins in congratulating her on her natal anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Shared with Canada Day I will add. On the merits, we say two things in response: First, it should not be the Prosecution's internal policy which dictates disclosure and these matters; it's the law. And in footnote 6 of our response which you have already, we cite the decision, the pre-trial decision of the Pre-Trial Chamber on the 8th of February, 2008, which makes it clear that we are entitled to full disclosure. Now, the Prosecution's addendum itself says that we should be wading through other trials to make sure that disclosure is complete. It's too much effort on their part to provide disclosure, and there's a jig-saw or some system of that sort that they rely on. But we say it's their burden to satisfy you that we have received full disclosure, and their addendum indicates that that has -- burden has not been met. So, therefore, that's one of the reasons that we ask you to -- we urge you to oppose the motion. We do set out our other reasons as well. But that's all I wish to say in response the disclosure issue. It's not policy of -- internal policy of the Prosecution which dictates what is full disclosure; it's the law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, I hadn't had the benefit of reading thoroughly your written submission which was filed, I think, only yesterday. But am I right to understand that the issue that is raised is -- at least one of the issues that are raised, is that reference to the cases to which your team has been given access and where you would be able to find the statements of the new witnesses that that reference in your view is insufficient and does not qualify as disclosure according to Rule 66(A)?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. What we're told is that somewhere in the disclosure to perhaps four other trials, somewhere in that disclosure, the material exists. Now, our submission is we shouldn't be expected to have to go wading through that material to identify it. And particularly now that we're in the trial, we're sitting on a regular basis, and it should be for the Prosecution to indicate to us where it is and whether we've received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. I understand. But, I mean, if you're given the name of the witnesses and the dates of which they testified in those other trials, wouldn't that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we're slightly at cross purposes at the moment. I think we mentioned that. But my understanding is, and I've just checked that, we've actually physically put onto a disc either the statement or the previous testimony on which we're relying. So we're not saying, Go and look for it. If you want anything else, we're saying, Go look for it, because you've got it all, or a lot of it. But I just confirmed that. We've actually physically handed over - not in paper but on disc - statement or transcript on which we've relied for the purposes of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The problem is that the -- the addendum indicates -- seems to indicate -- the Prosecution addendum seems to indicate that there is more to be done. That there's more coming our way. That there's more information that we have not had made available to us. And or response was based on that. That's our understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, there is. In a sense that -- Mr. O'Sullivan is quite right, and that's what we referred to. We don't simply say, Here's the statement, here's the previous testimony; we do full searches to see if they testified somewhere else, if they have made another statement. The thing that normally causes the problem, which is what we referred to in our motion, is that this database, which regrettably we gave the name of and has caused must hilarity amongst the Defence, isn't 100 per cent sure. Sometimes when witnesses have made earlier statements to the Bosnian authorities or to the Serbian authorities, it may not have got into that database, which is why we have to ask for this complete wider search of every possible, conceivable database that's available. This one contains the -- allegedly all the statements, but experience has shown us that occasionally it doesn't. So that's why we do the bigger search. But what I'm saying is the Defence are in a position to know now because they have been provided with the statement or the previous testimony of the witness on which we rely to cover the adjudicated fact. And our only caveat, our only problem at the moment, if you like, and I accept entirely that our internal problems are not to concern the Court, but only in so far as if Your Honours don't allow us to call the witnesses, and that's the difference. When we pick our witnesses for the 65 ter, subject to Your Honour's discretion, of course, we expect to be able to call them. So, of course, we provide everything; we do all the searches. Here, we don't know. So that's -- that's the reason that I'm saying this. But, as I say, it -- it's not right to say that they haven't been given the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To the extent that is it necessary for us to give a formal ruling or response, we will endeavor to do so in advance of -- well, as you point out, we aren't sitting tomorrow, but we would consider what has been said here. But having heard counsel, it appears that the differences are not as wide as they first appeared. And it's more a practical matter, working out what is -- what has, practically speaking, if that's not redundant, been disclosed to the Defence without having them to go on an safari to find whatever it is the Prosecution may be interested in. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, it boils down to a very simple, actually, issue, if I can sum it up this way: Are Your Honours going to order us, before making a ruling on which witnesses we can call, to make -- to do all the full searches and produce full disclosure? It's as simple as that. And that's -- that's what we'd ask for a ruling on. Because if Your Honours accede to what the Defence want, then we have to start straight away. Your Honour, the second matter is, I'm afraid, back -- it's allied because it's back to this business of challenging adjudicated facts. Yesterday, as His Honour Judge Delvoie asked Mr. Zecevic whether they were challenging the adjudicated fact in relation to a village called - and I hope I'm pronouncing it correctly - Davob -- I'll ask for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Dabovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Dabovci. Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic. Your Honours, we did a research through the -- I'm very grateful to the intern who did this research actually, as opposed to me, in which we found ten instances where specific adjudicated facts have been challenged through cross-examination, what's been put to witnesses since the trial began. And since virtually pre-trial, we have been discussing what happens when the Defence specifically challenge adjudicated facts, or the procedure. We argued this at some length on the 12th of May as to whether the Defence should be obliged to let us know now which adjudicated facts were the subject of specific challenge to witnesses. And Mr. Zecevic and I discussed the fact that the law says that it's for the Defence to raise the issue through calling reliable -- I've forgotten what the phrase is now - reliable and something-or-other evidence. Sorry, yes, we bring credible evidence - that's the word, thank you - to counter it. We got -- we discussed this in the Pre-Trial Conference, we've discussed this at various stages throughout the case, and Mr. Zecevic and, much earlier on, Mr. Pantelic said we challenge, blanket challenge, every single adjudicated fact. Mr. Krgovic was rather more circumstance -- and said, no, they would make it clear through cross-examination. And by and large that's right, and it's clear, as I said on the last occasion, that the Defence in fact do not challenge, or at least as far as one can gather, each and every adjudicated fact. There are certain specific ones that they challenge. But, Your Honour, I'm repeating my request that Your Honours make an order. We've got something like 27, we worked out, further witnesses to call, leaving out the other witnesses, to cover the adjudicated facts. We say -- we will have to apply, because of the ruling in Lukic and because we've put on notice, to add further witnesses. For example, Mr. Zecevic challenge's yesterday: We have a witness, that I personally happen to know about because I called him in Brdjanin, who can deal with that. We will now have to apply to call him. But the longer that they leave these challenges, the later our application is to call the witnesses. And so, Your Honour, I'm repeating my request that Your Honours order the Defence by the break - if possible, earlier - but by the break to tell us now, in terms, which adjudicated facts they are going to be putting specific challenges to witnesses about so that we can then apply, I'm afraid, but that's the -- the inevitable consequence, to call the witness who deals with it. Your Honour, I don't want to repeat everything we said on previous occasions, but that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will briefly state that I entirely disagree with the position of Ms. Korner, despite being her birthday and I join the congratulations. The fact is, Your Honours, we -- I didn't know that I was going to challenge that fact with the witness that came yesterday until the day before yesterday, because in his proofing note or a document, I found that the -- that the Prosecution asked him about that particular -- that particular incident or that particular village. And then he says, My family comes from that village, and I know it's a Serbian village, it's not a Muslim village. Before that point, it never crossed my mind that I would challenge that fact or that I would have a witness, the credible evidence, with which I will challenge that fact. We have the viva voce witnesses. The viva voce -- he might have said yesterday -- he comes to the Court, and while taking the general introduction -- during the general introduction he says, I come from the village of Dabovci. That would be -- that would trigger my interest in challenging that fact because how would I know that? I don't have the -- the opportunity to -- to interview all of them; or, if we do, we concentrate on the most important things. We don't -- we don't go all around the place and interview witnesses for days and days. Therefore, it is -- it is virtually impossible to -- to accept Ms. Korner's suggestion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, without going into the matter, I can tell you that your intern did a good job. Indeed, there are ten adjudicated facts challenged until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'll pass on Your Honours' congratulations. I repeat then. I'll pass on Your Honours' congratulations. I don't think there's anything I can add. I understand the position where, as Mr. Zecevic says, this was something they didn't think -- realise, but they must, in other cases - and it's clear in other cases because they have put specific documents or specific challenges - know which specific adjudicated facts they are challenging. You know, I accept, if something comes up, improvise, and you can't do anything about it. But if you have a clear instructions, the Defence know which witnesses are still left and what they're going to be challenging, then, Your Honours, I suggest that this is one of the times you really cannot sit on your powder and keep it dry, to mix my metaphors all over the place. Anyhow, Your Honours, I raise that. I mean, it may be something else that Your Honours might like to think about. But, Your Honours, can I make it absolutely clear: It is clear to us now that we will have to apply to call that witness. So, Your Honours, I don't expect to have complaints from the Defence if we apply only after we know to -- to call witnesses to cover challenged adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have to discuss this in some detail among the Judges. But as far as the question put to us by the Prosecution as to whether we will require the Prosecution, at this point, to start its full investigation, I think that would be a waste of resources. So we will hand down our decision shortly about which witnesses to call. And, as of that moment, you will know which witnesses to -- to do the continued search on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much, indeed. I'm very grateful. And if Your Honours would excuse me then, before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you please take the formal declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Could you make the solemn declaration again, please. There seems to be some slight technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may be seated. May the witness be handed the pseudonym sheet. If you're satisfied that that -- the contents of that document accurately discloses the particulars about yourself, you may sign it and hand it back to the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted under seal and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P1487, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, good morning to you, sir, and we thank you for coming to assist the Tribunal in your testimony. The piece of paper that you would have just signed is a part of the protective measures, -- is a feature of the protective measures which the Tribunal has granted in your case so that are you testifying under pseudonym and that your voice and features are distorted so that no one outside of the courtroom would be made aware of the fact that you have testified. That is one of the exceptional measures which the Chamber is authorised to allow in the case of certain witnesses where, for good and valid reasons, the Chamber is satisfied that such protective measures should be allowed. And it is exceptionally, because ordinarily the proceedings of this Tribunal are held in public in order to -- as a part of the -- as one of the components of a fair hearing to which the accused are entitled, and, beyond the interests of the accused, to satisfy the members of the public, particularly persons resident in the countries with which the proceedings of the Tribunal are concerned of the integrity -- of the proceedings. The pseudonym sheet that you would have signed has indicated your name and date of birth, so I needn't ask you about those. But I would ask your ethnicity and your profession. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, can I just raise one very brief matter. Can we deal with the issue of this witness's profession in privates session rather than with the -- the three protective measures. I think that would be safer. And there's another matter that I want to raise with you concerning private session with this particular witness. So I just think, as far as that second aspect of the question, it would be safer to do that in private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, what I would do, Mr. Di Fazio, is to leave that part of the question unanswered, and you can open with that when -- when you begin your -- your examination-in-chief. So would you tell us what your ethnicity is, sir? You may ignore the second part of the question I had asked about your profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Bosniak. I'm of Bosniak ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you testified previously in these proceedings or in proceedings in any of the countries that made up the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I would -- in that case, I need only remind you of the procedure of the Tribunal in that you have been called as a witness by one side - in this case, the Prosecution - and the other side, counsel for each of the two accused, would have a right to cross-examine you. And the Defence would -- the Prosecution would have a right to re-examine you, after which the Defence -- the Bench may have questions of you. Your testimony here is expected to be completed within today's sitting, which would end by 1.45. There are break that the -- that we have during that time to allow for the tapes to be changed and whatnot. The Prosecution has asked for an hour and a half to examine you; counsel for the accused Stanisic, one hour; and counsel for the accused Zupljanin, 15 minutes. Coming back to the matter of the breaks that we take, if, for any reason, you need a break other than that, if you would indicate to the Chamber, we would accommodate you. And I would invite Mr. Di Fazio to begin his examination-in-chief. And from what he's intimated already, we would move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we may as well break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is being escorted in, we would just say briefly, because we had indicated that we would use the break to consider the two matters raised by Ms. Korner on behalf of the Prosecution, that the -- in terms of the first issue, the Chamber has, in effect, ruled, as articulated by Judge Harhoff this morning. And in respect of the second matter, the problem about adjudicated facts is going to be an ongoing problem, and we do not appreciate that we can usefully say anything beyond what we would have said previously. And the -- we're in the process of researching the -- of searching the transcript to remind counsel of how we would have spoken to this when it was last raised. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Do Your Honours want any further submissions on that matter? Should I speak to Ms. Korner about the matter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I recall, Mr. Di Fazio, you had indicated we could move into open session. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. Thank you. Good. Can the witness please be shown 65 ter 3419.42.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise that place, that structure?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: I recognise it. It is Planina Kuca in the Semizovac settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- yes, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I tender that image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1488, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Now could we have 3419.36 on the screen, please. Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask to you look at that aerial shot and see if you can identify Planina Kuca or Planina's house on that particular aerial shot. And if you can, there's a pen that can you mark the screen. MR. DI FAZIO: I would be grateful if the usher could oversee that process. If the witness can just simply circle the screen, if he finds Planjo's house.

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: Yes, of course, this is Planjo's house. In this settlement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I tender that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. MR. DI FAZIO: And one more aerial photograph --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do apologise to the counsel. This is Exhibit P1489, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: I apologise to the Court. One more image, please, 65 ter 3419.38. If there's a problem, I can move on. If not, then ... thank you. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 3419.41.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise that place?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: This is the restaurant Sonja's Place in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it close to a railway -- is it close to a railway line?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is above the railway line, close to the Vogosca overpass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it also have another name, Kontiki [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was called Kontiki, but it was better known and more popular as the Sonja's Place. MR. DI FAZIO: Now, I seek to tender that into evidence, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1490, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Along that railway line that you're talking about, were there wartime structures at various intervals, built, I think, by the Germans during the Second World War, known as bunkers?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: Yes, there were such structures. These were bunkers from the Second World War which had been built by the Wehrmacht soldiers, German soldiers. And from Ploce to Bosanski Samac there are such bunkers in the intervals at each -- 10 to 15 kilometres. And they were meant to secure the railway line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there such a bunker close Sonja's place or Kontiki?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There is one very close to this restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown 65 ter 3419.43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. This is an aerial shot. Having -- looking at that aerial shot, can you tell us if Sonja's Place and the bunker are visible. And if they, if they are, could you indicate them with two circles around their structures?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: Yes, you can see them. I can recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you put a circle around Sonja's place?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: It's this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can see the bunker, can you indicate where that is?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: It is this structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So the small -- the larger circle on that image is Sonja's and the smaller image is the bunker. MR. DI FAZIO: And I tender that image.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1491, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks. 65 ter 3419.39, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate, if you can see in that photograph, the SJB building in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: I can see it, and I can do it. And the building of the public security station is located in the building of the Municipal Assembly in Vogosca. And this is the building. Can I circle it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-155
utterances.text: It's this building over here. On the right hand is the entrance to the Municipal Assembly; and on the left side is the entrance to the public security station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: And I tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1492, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, I think that at this point we should go back into private session, just because of the nature of the questions that I'm going to now ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And can we keep that image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we -- as would have been previously indicated to you, we now rise for the day. And, indeed, this concludes our sittings for the rest of the week. We would resume in this courtroom on Monday morning -- sorry, in Courtroom III on Monday morning at 9.00. And I'm obliged to point out to you that, having been sworn as a witness, you cannot communicate with counsel from either side; or in -- and in such conversations as you have with persons outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we adjourn until Monday morning, and I wish everyone a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
